title: How To Encourage Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin lays out two narrow, deliberately unemotional ways to encourage difficult students as they make progress under an SCM approach. The first, "real praise," must respond to genuine, sustained improvement over time rather than a single good hour or day, and should be delivered flatly and matter-of-factly rather than effusively. The second, "real words," consists of brief, sincere lines of encouragement — like "I believe in you" — offered without sentimentality, since he claims difficult students can detect phoniness instantly and reject anything that sounds babyish or condescending. His central argument is that emotional restraint, not warmth, is what makes praise and encouragement land with students who have been fed years of false, inflated praise as a management tactic. He closes by insisting that difficult students require relentless long-term commitment from a teacher who refuses to give up, even when meaningful change takes far longer than expected.
points: "Real praise" must respond to actual, sustained behavioral improvement — never just a single good hour or day.
Both praise and encouragement should be delivered flatly and matter-of-factly, since difficult students can spot phoniness instantly.
Brief, sincere lines like "I believe in you" are said to carry more weight precisely because they're rare and restrained.
Difficult students are described as needing relentless, long-term commitment from a teacher who never gives up on them.
quotes: One of the best things you can do for difficult students is put a stop to the years of false praise they’ve been showered with.
Not a good hour or even a good day. Your praise must be in response to actual leveling up of behavior.
That’s it. Simple. Matter-of-fact. Don’t be effusive or over-the-top. Tell them the truth, nothing more.
But again, you can’t be emotional. Your words and tone mustn’t be babyish or condescending.
The prickly pears need you to never give up on them. They need you desperately to see it through for their long-term future, regardless of how long it takes.
